text: A fast local inference engine for Inkling 2 Mini on Apple silicon, written in Rust and built for coding agents. It serves an OpenAI-compatible API that Codex, aider and opencode can use as they would a hosted model. It runs one model family and does not try to be general. That is what lets it do things a general engine does not: generate whole tokens in one GPU submission, keep processed prompts between requests and restarts, and copy runs of tokens the reply repeats from the conversation. rustling chat running on an M1 Max with 64 GB. Watch it on asciinema . cargo install --path cli rustling chat The first run downloads Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_M conversion (16.6 GB) to the Hugging Face cache, where other tools that use the Hub will find it too. rustling pull does only that, if you would rather fetch it ahead. A download that is interrupted starts again from the beginning; on an unreliable connection, hf download unsloth/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF Inkling-2-Mini-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf can resume, and rustling finds the file it leaves. To serve it to other programs: rustling serve curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H ' content-type: application/json ' -d ' { "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}], "reasoning_effort": "low", "stream": true } ' Usage Chat rustling chat is an assistant for the current directory, with the model in the same process: no server, no network. It can read and search files ( read , grep and glob ), asking before each call; it changes nothing and runs no commands. It is built on manifatura, an agent framework. Its own instructions are one line, cli/src/agent/system.md ; the tools' guidelines, the AGENTS.md files, the directory and the date follow it. rustling chat # a new session rustling chat --continue # the latest session in this directory rustling chat --resume # list this directory's sessions rustling chat --resume 019aa1b2c3d4-5e6f7a8b # continue one of them rustling chat --yes # read and search without asking rustling chat --effort high # think longer before answering rustling chat --system " Answer in French. " # add to the agent's instructions rustling chat --logs # keep the log, behind a `logs` button rustling chat --context 32768 --max-tokens 8192 # a larger window and longer replies Its instructions follow the AGENTS.md convention: ~/.config/rustling/AGENTS.md , then AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md ) in each directory from the repository root down to the current one. Sessions are kept per directory under ~/.local/share/rustling/sessions . Processed prompts are kept as serve keeps them ( --cache-gb , --cache-dir , --no-cache-dir ), so a resumed session, even after a restart, starts in seconds. The chat can use the tools of MCP servers, reached at a URL (streamable HTTP) or run on this machine (stdio), set up in ~/.config/rustling/mcp.toml . For Exa 's web search, through its hosted server: [ servers . exa ] url = " https://mcp.exa.ai/mcp " env_headers = { x-api-key = " EXA_API_KEY " } # optional: without a key, Exa's free rate limit applies eager = true # offer its tools directly A local server is a command , with args , env and cwd ; an HTTP one takes headers and env_headers . Servers start while the model loads; one that does not start is reported and left out. A server's tools are named <server>__<tool> . Without eager they are kept out of the prompt, which matters with a small context window, and the model finds them with find_tools and runs them with run_tool . approve = true asks before each call. /mcp lists the servers and their tools. The conversation goes into the terminal's own scrollback, so it scrolls, selects and copies like any output. Below it, the screen shows the reply as it is written, the input, and a line of statistics: how much of the context window is in use, how many prompt tokens were new and how many reused, and how fast the last prompt and reply went. There is no log unless you ask for one with --logs (at --log-level ). Then a logs button at the end of the statistics opens it; click it, or press Ctrl-L. The button needs the mouse, so with --logs the scroll wheel goes to rustling instead of scrolling the terminal, and selecting text needs the modifier your terminal uses for that (Option in iTerm2 and Terminal.app, Shift in most others). Typing / lists the commands: /mcp lists the MCP servers, /new starts a new session, /resume ID switches to another, /sessions lists them, /compact [focus] summarises older messages to make room, /effort shows or sets how much the model reasons, and /exit quits. /effort off stops the reasoning altogether, as --no-reasoning does, and /effort high (or any level) brings it back. The effort is part of the prompt, so the reply after a change processes the conversation again. --effort is how much the model reasons before it replies: none , minimal , low , medium , high , xhigh or max , or a number from 0 to 0.99. Even none leaves a little reasoning: the model was built that way, and its makers say so. To have none at all: rustling chat --no-reasoning # answers start at once rustling serve --no-reasoning # for every request This keeps the model from ever opening a reasoning block. Answers come sooner and are less considered, and a model that cannot reason is less inclined to call tools: asked for the weather with a weather tool on hand, it offered to look instead of looking. Leave it off for coding agents. rustling generate " Write a function that reverses a linked list. " --effort low rustling generate " Write a haiku about rivers. " --temperature 0.7 --top-p 0.95 --seed 1 rustling generate " What is 17 * 23? " --temperature 0 # always the most likely token rustling generate " Hello " --timing # where the time went Server rustling serve # http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 rustling serve --port 9000 --host 0.0.0.0 # reachable from other machines rustling serve --context 32768 --max-tokens 8192 # a larger window and longer replies rustling serve --cache-gb 16 # keep up to 16 GiB of processed prompts rustling serve --cache-dir /Volumes/fast/rustling # keep them somewhere else rustling serve --no-cache-dir # keep them in memory only rustling serve --temperature 0.2 --top-p 0.9 # sampling for requests that do not set their own rustling serve --log-level debug # also report progress through long prompts A typical setup for a coding agent: rustling serve --context 32768 The server's flags are defaults. A request sets its own temperature , top_p , top_k , seed , max_tokens and stop , and its reasoning effort, which is not a server flag: curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H ' content-type: application/json ' -d ' { "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Is 91 prime?"}], "reasoning_effort": "high", "max_tokens": 2000 } ' Reasoning comes back as reasoning_content , apart from the answer. GET /v1/models names the model and GET /health says the server is up. rustling pull # fetch the default model ahead of time rustling pull thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini # the published checkpoint, 19 GB rustling chat --model thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini # run it rustling serve --model ~ /models/Inkling-2-Mini-Q4_K_M.gguf # a file you already have RUSTLING_MODEL=thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini rustling chat # or by environment Without the GPU rustling chat --backend cpu rustling pull --draft && rustling chat --backend cpu --draft # the draft model helps on the CPU Coding agents The server speaks POST /v1/chat/completions and POST /v1/responses , with streaming and tool calls. An agent's opening prompt is long (10,000 tokens and more) and takes a minute or two the first time. The server keeps what it has processed, in memory and under ~/.cache/rustling , so after that a new session starts in a few seconds, also after a restart. Give the agent a long timeout: nothing is sent while a long prompt is being processed. Codex # ~/.codex/config.toml [ model_providers . rustling ] name = " Rustling " base_url = " http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 " wire_api = " responses " stream_idle_timeout_ms = 1800000 stream_max_retries = 0 request_max_retries = 0 [ profiles . rustling ] model_provider = " rustling " model = " inkling-2-mini " codex exec --profile rustling " Read the README and summarise this project. " aider aider --model openai/inkling-2-mini --openai-api-base http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 --openai-api-key rustling --timeout 1800 opencode and anything else that takes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint: point it at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 with the model name inkling-2-mini . To try experimental split attention for long-context GGUF generation, build with cargo build --release --features split-attention and run target/release/rustling with a context window large enough for the prompt and reply (for example, serve --context 65536 ). It splits full attention across blocks of cached keys on the same GPU when generating one token with at least 32,768 visible keys. Prompt processing in large batches and speculative verification batches use the usual kernels. The different order of floating-point sums can change a reply. The following measurements use the previous LM Studio Q4_K_M conversion. On an M1 Max with 64 GB, against llama.cpp running the same file: On an M4 Max, generation in a short conversation runs at about 50 tokens/s. In an agent session, most turns add a few hundred tokens to a conversation the server already holds, and those take 3 to 10 seconds before the reply starts. Replies that repeat text from the conversation, as edits to a file do, go faster than the figures above. The LM Studio Q4_K_M conversion was used for the measurements below. The GPU computes in a different arithmetic from the CPU, so each way of running it was scored against the published checkpoint: how often it picks the same most likely next token. The first row is the checkpoint itself in another, equally valid arithmetic, which shows how much disagreement is ordinary. Where the checkpoint gives its choice a probability of 90% or more, every row agrees with it at least 98% of the time, and on the model's own writing none of them ever disagreed. Perplexity is the same to within 2%. The conversion costs a point or two of agreement; running it on the GPU costs nothing measurable beyond that. tests/quality.rs reproduces this on text of your choosing. Everything has a default; these are the ones worth knowing. rustling <command> --help lists the rest. The model takes up to 1,048,576 tokens, but time grows with the context, so the default is sized for the chip: a prompt that fills the window should still be processed in about two minutes. Only the M1 figure is measured (on an M1 Max). The others scale it by each generation's GPU and are estimates; measurements are welcome. --context sets any size you like. Each token of context costs 64 KB of memory, on top of a fixed 0.3 GB. A prompt that does not fit is refused with a message saying so, and a reply stops when the window is full. Logs go to stderr through tracing . At info , the server reports each request: the size of its prompt, how much of it was reused, how long the rest took and at what speed, and the reply's length and speed in tokens per second. [3] 8 messages, 11 tools, 12891 prompt tokens [3] prompt: 12615 tokens reused, 276 processed in 5.7s (48 tokens/s) [3] reply: 164 tokens in 8.5s (19.4 tokens/s), stop; copied: 3 of 21 proposed tokens accepted in 10 rounds --log-level debug adds progress through long prompts, warn keeps only problems, and off is silent. The GGUF loader reads F32, BF16, NVFP4, Q4_K, Q5_0, Q5_K, Q6_K and Q8_0 tensors. docs/internals.md describes each part and what it measured: the GPU token path, prompt processing, reuse of processed prompts, copying from the context, the draft model, the checkpoint's native formats, and how the engine is tested against the reference implementation. The workspace has two crates: the engine as a library ( rustling , at the root), and the rustling command ( rustling-cli , in cli/ ), which uses only the library's public API. src/ the library engine/ the model thread: requests in, events out, the prompt cache kept generate/ sessions, sampling, copying, the draft model, the prompt cache model/ the layers and the state they keep gpu/ Metal: kernels, prompt paths, shaders weights/ checkpoint and GGUF formats, downloads cli/src/ the command cli/ the commands server/ the HTTP API, over the engine Development cargo test --release # the tests that need a model skip when it is not downloaded uv run tools/golden.py --help # reference outputs from the transformers implementation Privacy rustling contacts the Hugging Face Hub to download models and nothing else.
